newsitem.title: IRAN: Iran's hopeful youth become president-makers.
newsitem.headline: Iran's hopeful youth become president-makers.

text.p: The children of the Iranian revolution have emerged as a key force in Iranian politics after guaranteeing the election of moderate Shi'ite cleric Mohammad Khatami as the country's next president.

The huge vote that Khatami secured from those born just before and after Iran's turbulent 1979 Islamic revolution was a crucial factor in lifting the former culture minister to the country's highest elective office, Iran-watchers said.
Khatami's appeal as an educated, potential social reformer grabbed the hearts of many of Tehran's young who complain of limited freedoms under Iran's strict Islamist leadership.
As a voting block, Khatami won over the right people as some 60 percent of Iran's 60 million people are under 30 years old, a potential demographic timebomb for future Iranian leaders.

In central Tehran's Student Park and around Tehran University -- once the home of radical Islamist students who stormed the U.S. embassy and held staff members hostage for 444 days -- the young are saying that it is time for change.

"Young people voted for Khatami because we wanted a change. He represents a ray of hope for us...If he keeps his promises he will definitely change our lives," said 21-year-old Maryam, a graphics student.

"In the sphere of economics, I do not have many great expectations. But politically and culturally I expect him to provide more freedom," said Ebrahim Rostami, 24, a political science graduate at a local university.

Freedom for Tehran's youth is a broad concept covering anything from the right to wear jeans at university, a more relaxed dress code for women and access to satellite television to the creation of political parties and more job opportunities.

Khatami's supporters are also hopeful that he will have a powerful mandate to try to ease the state's intrusive checks on daily life and to help young people find employment, check rising prices and improve Iran's battered ties with the world.

Young women aged around 20 on at least one main Tehran highway were detained on Saturday evening by police for breaking dress codes which demand that women cover themselves and refrain from using makeup.

Attempts by young people to celebrate Khatami's victory on Tehran's traffic-jammed streets were blocked by police and religious groups discouraged celebrations because they coincided with a Shi'ite mourning period.

"The rights of the young people are not observed in this country. The fact that Khatami was elected with this high vote indicated he might be able to slowly change the system step by step," said Pouya, 20, a Tehran university student.
"Khatami is our best hope for more freedom, to give us respect. At times we were treated as criminals by the police," said Babak, a 21-year-old student.
Many of Tehran's young were turned off by Khatami's main rival conservative Parliamentary Speaker Ali Akbar Nateq-Nouri whom they expected to clamp down further on social liberty.

"Khatami will not be able to solve inflation in just four years but we do expect him to pay attention to the problems of the young people in helping them find employment," said Davood Fathi, a graduate in forestry economics.
His popularity was evident in the final election figures when he reaped 20.1 million of nearly 30 million votes cast on Friday. Nateq-Nouri, the establishment's candidate, got 7.2 million votes.

Khatami, a 54-year-old theologian, has lived in Europe and speaks German, English and Arabic. He will replace President Akbar Hashemi Rafsanjani who steps down in August after serving the two four-year terms allowed under the Iranian constitution.
Rafsanjani told a news conference in Tehran on Sunday that the youth vote had played its role in Khatami's election.
